Within the first two weeks after weaning, piglets may develop severe
diarrhea, leading to dehydration and, in some cases, death. This is a
problem affecting swine industry worldwide, including Brazil, where
post-weaning diarrhea is prevalent in most far ms during this critical
phase [4].
Post-weaning diarrhea can lead to intestinal dysbiosis, driven by
dietary, social, and environmental changes that disrupt microbiota
balance and weaken the piglets’ immune system [5]. During this phase,
piglets exhibit several physiological limitations, including insufficient
production of digestive enzymes, reduced nutrient absorption due to
villous underdevelopment, immature gastric secretion, and low feed
intake. These factors contribute to the growth limitations commonly
observed during this period [ 6].
In addition, piglets become more susceptible to infections, promot -
ing the proliferation of pathogenic bacteria such as Escherichia coli ,
Clostridium perfringens , Salmonella choleraesuis , and Salmonella enterica
subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium. At the same time, there is a
reduction in the populations of beneficial bacteria, such as Lactobacillus
sobrius, L. acidophilus, and L. reuteri (Silva et al., 2018). These alterations can
have significant consequences, including weight loss and impaired
growth, ultimately affecting swine production efficiency [ 7].
The intestinal microbiota plays an essential role in food degradation
and fermentation, as well as in pathogen defense through competition
for nutrients and adhesion sites and the secretion of antimicrobial
peptides [8]. This protective function, known as colonization resistance,
helps shield the host from infections [9]. The microbiota composition is
influenced by various factors and differs under different management
conditions. Understanding the pig microbiota and its diversity not only
may enhance production quality but also provide insight into the de -
terminants of health and disease in pigs and other species they interact
with, including humans [ 10]. Studies on post -weaning diarrhea and its
association with specific microorganisms, such as Escherichia coli and
Salmonella Typhimurium, have been conducted in multiple countries
[11,12]. In Brazil, research on weaned pigs has primarily focused on
animal performance and stress responses, particularly in states like
Santa Catarina and Sa ˜o Paulo [13,14].
Investigating animal microbiota across different production systems
and regions is essential for understanding its role in post -weaning
diarrhea. In Brazil, few studies have examined this condition in field -
raised pigs, and none have focused on animals from Rio Grande do Sul.
This study aimed to identify microbial taxa associated with intes - tinal
dysbiosis in weaned piglets on a farm in this state. By analyzing fecal
samples, we compared the microbial structure of piglets with diarrhea
to that of healthy counterparts, providing a detailed insight into fecal
microbiota composition during this critical phase.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Ethics Committee and approval

This study was approved by the Ethics Committee for the Use of
Animals of the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul (CEUA -UFRGS),
under approval number 33558/2018. All procedures involving the an -
imals were carried out in accordance with animal welfare standards,
aiming to minimize any discomfort and suffering during the experiment.

2.2. Experimental design and sample collection

Samples from post -weaning pigs with diarrhea (n = 15, diarrhea
group) and pigs without diarrhea (n = 15, control group) were obtained
by convenience. Diarrhea was determined by the presence of liquid
stools and the number of samples was defined based on the number of
piglets with diarrhea at the time of collection (n = 15). To ensure
equivalence between the groups, the same number of samples was
randomly collected from healthy piglets. The diarrhea piglets were all
housed in the same pen, while the healthy piglets were housed in 10
animals/pen. The animals were from Duroc breed and in both groups,
were 33 days old and in the nursery phase. The animals were sourced
from a Certified Swine Breeding Farms (CSBF) in Rio Grande do Sul,
south Brazil.
In the transition phase from milk to solid food (around 15 days of
age), the animals received a pre -starter feed. Although we did not had
access to exact feed formula, this kind of feed in Brazil usually contains
highly digestible ingredients like fish meal, powdered milk, soy, and
corn, along with vitamins, minerals, and additives for intestinal health
and weight gain. Probiotics, prebiotics, and antioxidants are also
included to support the microbiota an d immune system.
At weaning, 28 -day-old piglets were subjected to the following im -
munization plan: autogenous vaccine against Actinobacillus pleuro -
pneumoniae (Microvet, Brazil), M + PAC against Mycoplasma
hyopneumoniae (MSD Animal Health, USA), and Circumvent PCV against
porcine circovirus type 2 (PCV2; MSD Animal Health, USA). In addition,
as part of farm management, all animals received antibiotic treatment
with Norfloxacin 14 mg/kg (Farmaflox®, Farmabase™, Brazil) added to
the drinking water at 21 days for seven consecutive days and Tula -
thromycin a single dose of 2.5 mg/kg of body weight administered
intramuscularly (Draxin®, Zoetis ™, USA).
Piglets that exhibited diarrhea symptoms were housed in a separate
pen from the other animals. To avoid environmental contamination and
for the sake of animal welfare, rectal swabs were collected from the pigs
with clinical signs of diarrhea (n = 15) and from animals that did not
have diarrhea (n = 15). The swabs were placed in sterile tubes con-
taining 400 μl of RNALater® (ThermoFisher Scientific, USA). The swabs
were transported from the farm to the laboratory on ice on the same day of
collection and subsequently stored at —70 ◦C until sample processing.

2.3. DNA extraction and 16S rRNA partial gene amplification

Before DNA extraction, the samples were homogenized using a
Precellys®24 (Bertin Technologies S.A.S, France). Microbial DNA was
extracted using the MagMax Pathogen DNA/RNA kit (Thermo Fisher
Scientific, USA) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The V4 re-
gion of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene was amplified by PCR (94 ◦C for 2
min, followed by 35 cycles of 94 ◦C for 30 s, 55 ◦C for 30 s, and 68 ◦C for
45 s, with a final extension at 68 ◦C for 5 min) using 16S-forward (5′ TCG
TCG GCA GCG TCA GAT GTG TAT AAG AGA CAG GTG CCA GCM GCC
GCC GCG GTA 3′) and reverse (5′ GTC TCG TGG GCT CGG AGT TGT GTA
TAA GAG ACA GGG ACT ACH VGG GTW TCT AAT 3′) primers, which
contain the Illumina adapter sequence (Kozich et al., 2013). The re-
actions were performed using Phusion polymerase and 12.5 ng of DNA,
following the standard protocol for this enzyme. The amplicons were
purified using Agencourt AMPure XP magnetic beads (Beckman Coulter,
USA) and indexed according to the Illumina protocol. The libraries were
quantified using a Qubit 2.0 fluorometer (Invitrogen, USA), and the
concentrations were normalized for sequencing, which was performed
using the MiSeq Reagent Kit v2 500 cycles (2 × 250 paired-end) on the
MiSeq sequencer (Illumina, USA).

2.4. Bioinformatics analysis

The sequence data was processed using a pipeline from CLC Geno-
mics Workbench software version 23.0.4 (QIAGEN, DEU), following
manufacturer instructions for microbiome analysis. Initially, the se -
quences underwent quality analysis and were trimmed to remove in -
dexes and adapters. A quality filter with a Phred score lower than 20 was
used to eliminate low-quality reads, and potentially chimeric sequences
were identified and removed.
After the initial filtering and trimming steps, the remaining se -
quences were clustered into Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) based
on a 99 % identity level and classified against the SILVA v138 reference
database [15]. Microbial communities were analyzed, in which alpha

diversity, beta diversity, taxonomic distribution, and differential abun -
dance analyses were conducted. Functional profiling was analyzed using
PICRUST2 software [ 16] with a MetaCyc database [ 17] which has a
broader and more complete set of metabolic pathway data [ 18].

2.5. Statistical analyses

The microbial alpha diversity of the samples was determined using
abundance-based coverage estimation (ACE), Chao1 diversity index,
Faith’s phylogenetic diversity (PD), Simpson index, and Shannon index.
For statistical comparisons of these indexes, a Mann Whitney test was
applied. Beta diversity indices of the microbial samples were determined
using principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) based on Bray -Curtis
dissimilarity, UniFrac phylogenetic diversity, and Jaccard similarity
index. To obtain statistical confidence in the observed sample clustering
by PCoA, permutation multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) was
performed on the distance matrix. For differential abundance, a
generalized linear model (GLM) was used to analyze differences in
feature abundance (taxa or metabolic pathways) across sample groups.
It assumes Negative Binomial distribution for abundances and applied
the Likelihood Ratio test for group-wide comparisons. Features with P <
0.05 were considered enriched.

3. Results

3.1. Quality analysis and trimming

The sequences were imported into the CLC platform, where the
quality analysis of the 30 samples was performed, followed by trimming. Two
sequences from the diarrhea group were removed due to a small number
of reads after trimming (5D: 48,128 and 11D: 800). The remaining
sequences were then composed of 15 from the control group and 13 from
the diarrhea group, totaling 28 sequences ( Supplementary Table 1 ).
3.2. Taxonomic analysis

A total of 40,335 bacterial taxa (OTUs) belonging to 27 phyla, 157
families, 397 genera and 634 species were identified ( Supplementary
Table 2 ). In addition, 142 genera and 948 species were identified as
nonclassified taxons. The most frequent phyla were Bacillota (57 % and
65 %), Bacteroidota (17 % and 16 %), Pseudomonadota (14 % and 7 %) in the
control and diarrhea groups, respectively, and Campylobacteriota (6
%) in both groups. The most abundant families were Lactobacillaceae,
Lachnospiraceae, Prevotellaceae, Veillonellaceae, Ruminococcaceae, and
Oscillospiraceae in both groups ( Fig. 1 ). The ratio between Bacillota/
Bacteriodota was 3.35 in the control group and 4.06 in the diarrhea group,
which may indicate dysbiosis.

3.3. Microbial diversity

There were no statistically significant differences between the con -
trol and diarrhea groups in any of the evaluated indices: Chao1 (p =
0.525), Simpson (p = 0.717), and Shannon (p = 0.683) ( Fig. 2 A).
Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) based on Bray-Curtis dissimilarity
(p = 0.353; Fig. 2B), Jaccard (p = 0.414), weighted UniFrac (p = 0.510), and
unweighted UniFrac (p = 0.390) also indicated no statistically sig-
nificant differences between the groups.

3.4. Differential abundance analysis

Only one enriched phylum was found, Patescibacteria, in the control
group. The families enriched in the control group included Aceto- bacteraceae,
Pseudomonadaceae, Saccharimonadaceae, Erwiniaceae, Alteromonadaceae,
Mycobacteriaceae, Carnobacteriaceae, Enterobacteri- aceae, and only the
family Fusobacteriaceae in the diarrhea group (Fig. 3A). Regarding the
genera, in the diarrhea group, the differentially abundant genera were
Rheinheimera, Candidatus, Saccharimonas, Pan- toea, Massilia,
Pseudomonas, Gluconacetobacter, Cloacibacillus, Glucono- bacter,
Oenococcus, Acetobacter, Komagataeibacter, and Liquorilactobacillus. In the
control group, they were Pasteurella, Anaero- biospirillum, Atopobium,

3.5. Metabolic functional prediction

In the analyzed groups, a total of 13 metabolic pathways differen -
tially present in the analyzed groups were identified. In the diarrhea
group, three pathways related to the degradation of aromatic com -
pounds (2 -aminophenol, 4 -chloronitrobenzene, and 4 -nitrotoluene II),
novobiocin biosynthesis (secondary metabolite biosynthesis), manosyl-
fructose biosynthesis (carbohydrate biosynthesis), and energetic meta -
bolism (reductive tricarboxylic acid cycle) were identified to be
overrepresented when compared to control group. On the other hand, in
the control group, five pathways related to amino acid degradation
(trans-3-hydroxy-L-proline, L-lysine, L-threonine I, and two
superpathways, L -threonine and L -lysine), carbohydrate degradation
(trehalose III), and fermentation ((S) -propano-1,2-diol) were enriched
(Fig. 4).

4. Discussion

Characterizing the intestinal microbiota of suckling piglets is
important for production, as it can help to predict the occurrence and
severity of post-weaning diarrhea and influence growth performance in
adulthood [ 19]. In this study, taxonomic analysis of gut microbiota se -
quences revealed a predominance of Bacillota, followed by Bacteroidota
and Pseudomonadota in both groups. These phyla have been highlighted
as the major constituents of swine intestine, regardless of age [20]. Other
commonly present phyla include Actinomycetota and Spirochaetes [6,21].
While the overall taxonomic profile remains stable, microbial shifts
below the phylum level can occur in response to intestinal

The most frequent families in our research were Lactobacillaceae ,
Lachnospiraceae, Prevotellaceae, Veollonellaceae, Ruminococcaceae, and
Oscillospiraceae in both groups. Some, like Prevotellaceae, include bac- teria
that metabolize plant polysaccharides and glycans, likely adapting to
dietary changes in weaned piglets [22]. Others, such as Veillonellaceae or
Oscillospiraceae, can utilize minor compounds like plant mono -
saccharides (e. g. tagatose) or microbial fermentation byproducts like
lactate, converting them into short-chain fatty acids [1]. The dominance
of Lactobacillaceae, Lachnospiraceae, and Ruminococcaceae during the post-
weaning phase has also been reported in previous studies, which
observed that stress associated with the weaning transition resulted in
episodes of diarrhea and reduced growth [ 23].
Regarding the bacterial communities, no significant differences in
alpha and beta diversity metrics were observed between the groups,
meaning that no overall diversity shifts occurred in the evaluated ani -
mals. The exclusive use of rectal swabs for sample collection limited the
identification of the specific origin of diarrhea. Additionally, affected
animals were separated at symptoms onset, introducing potential bias
due to variability in the timing of diarrhea manifestation. It is important
to point out that all animals, regardless of group, were from the same
breed, were at the same growth phase, received the same feed and fol -
lowed the same vaccination and antibiotic therapy [24] protocols on the
farm, which may have influenced microbial diversity. Although this is a
limitation, it also allows us to access the reality of a field situation.
Studies have shown that pigs receiving prophylactic antibiotics
exhibit lower bacterial diversity, suggesting that these compounds alter
the intestinal microbiota. Furthermore, antibiotic use in the pre - and
postnatal period has been associated with reduced microbial diversity
and an increased frequency of antibiotic -resistant bacteria, potentially
leading to dysbiosis [25]. Research also indicates that antibiotics induce
rapid shifts in gut microbiota composition, with changes detectable
within two days in the ileum and within seven days in feces [26]. These
factors may have contributed to the lack of differences in microbial di -
versity between the analyzed groups and the persistence of diarrhea.
The use of antibiotics in livestock for prophylaxis and growth pro -
motion contributes to antimicrobial resistance and environmental
contamination, posing risks to animal, human, and ecosystem health
[27]. To address this, the WHO launched the Global Antimicrobial
Resistance and Use Surveillance System (GLASS) in 2015, alongside
initiatives from the OIE and FAO to combat resistant pathogens [69,70].
In Brazil, the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MAPA)
implemented the second phase of the National Action Plan for Antimi-
crobial Resistance (PAN-BR AGRO) (2023–2027) to mitigate its impact
on agriculture and public health [ 28]. In accordance with that, recent
studies highlight alternatives like essential oils, prebiotics, probiotics,
and zinc oxide as effective antibiotic replacements, promoting gut health
and improving piglet performance [ 24,29,30]. These findings support
reducing or eliminating antibiotics in pig farming as a viable strategy to
curb antimicrobial resistance. Therefore, studies like ours can help in
understanding the changes in the intestinal microbiota related to
postweaning diarrhea and potentially provide new insights to produce
alternatives to antibiotics.
Despite the absence of significant differences in alpha and beta di -
versities, differential abundance analysis revealed that one phylum and
eight bacterial families were enriched in the control group, whereas only
one family was enriched in the diarrhea group. Additionally, 12 genera
were enriched in the diarrhea group and 16 in the control group. These
findings suggest that dysbiosis may be present to some extent and could
be associated with post -weaning diarrhea in pigs. Other studies have
also reported no significant changes in alpha and beta diversity under
diarrhea conditions in weaning pigs [ 31], suggesting that not always
global microbiota alterations are observed in different health conditions,
as it is often a stable structure. However, subtle shifts in microbial
composition can still be detected. Notably, most of the enriched taxa
were not among the top 10 most abundant in the evaluated microbiota.
Research has shown that low -abundance microbial populations play a
key role in pathogen -host interactions [ 67]. Even in small quantities,
intestinal commensal bacteria contribute significantly to immune sys -
tem development. These findings highlight their crucial role in immune
maturation and modulation despite their low prevalence.
In the control group, the superphylum Patescibacteria was enriched.
These ultra-small bacteria have a simplified genome, unusual ribosomal
compositions, and sometimes intron sequences within 16S rRNA genes, a rare
feature in bacteria [32]. They are highly diverse and inhabit various
ecosystems but have limited cellular synthesis capability [ 33]. Most
cultured Patescibacteria live as obligate epibionts, adhering to and
proliferating on other bacteria [ 36]. A Danish study identified Patesci-
bacteria as one of the most abundant phyla in the colons of pigs,
regardless of colonic inflammation [ 35]. Similarly, a Chinese study on
pig microbiota reported Patescibacteria as highly abundant in healthy
animals [34]. These findings align with our results, as both the Chinese
study and ours observed a high prevalence of this phylum in healthy
pigs. Although the Danish study also detected Patescibacteria in pigs with

colonic inflammation, the consistent association between this phylum
and health in multiple studies supports its potential role in maintaining
gut homeostasis.
In the diarrhea group, the Fusobacteriaceae family was enriched.
Fusobacteria are known for their inflammatory potential, triggering host
immune responses against pathogens. While inflammation is essential
for homeostasis, infection defense, and tissue repair, uncontrolled
inflammation can lead to cell damage and contribute to chronic diseases
and cancer. Fusobacterium, particularly Fusobacterium nucleatum , is
linked to colorectal cancer and inflammatory bowel disease in humans
and is frequently detected in intestinal lesions and feces [37]. In piglets
infected with porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV), increased Fuso-
bacterium levels exacerbate intestinal inflammation [ 38]. This bacterium
damages the epithelial barrier and worsens diarrhea by inducing
pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-1α [39]. Luo et al. [40] reported
a higher abundance of Fusobacterium in pigs during the weaning phase,
noting that its presence can be up to four times greater in pigs with
diarrhea than in healthy individuals. These findings support the asso -
ciation between Fusobacterium and intestinal inflammation, potentially
explaining its presence in diarrheic piglets in our study.
The genus Liquorilactobacillus , enriched in the control group, has
probiotic properties, including microbiota regulation, colitis relief, and
strong antimicrobial activity [ 41]. Additionally, Komagataeibacter, Ace-
tobacter, and Gluconobacter were enriched in this group. These genera
produce bacterial cellulose by fermenting acetic acid and converting
sugars like glucose, fructose, and sucrose [42,68]. The presence of these
enriched genera in the control group suggests a potential protective role
against diarrhea.
Other enriched genera in the control group were Escherichia/Shigella.
These bacteria are naturally abundant in the piglet gut during the
suckling phase, when the immune system is developing. While some
species are opportunistic pathogens [43], maternal IgA antibodies from
milk protect piglets against infections [ 19]. Salmonella, another patho -
genic genus enriched in the control group, often causes asymptomatic
infections in pigs, allowing prolonged fecal shedding [ 44]. As a major
cause of foodborne illness worldwide, Salmonella from pork products is
estimated to account for 15 –23% of human salmonellosis cases in
Europe [45]. Its ability to persist as a commensal in livestock compli -
cates detection and control efforts [ 45,46].
The genus Pseudomonas was enriched in the control group. While
primarily a respiratory pathogen, it has been detected in the gut of mice
with dysbiosis, where Bacteroidota and Bacillota help to prevent
P. aeruginosa colonization, whereas Proteobacteria promote it [47]. In
pigs, respiratory infections caused by Pseudomonas, Bordetella, and
Burkholderia can trigger gastrointestinal symptoms, like diarrhea, stim-
ulating the immune system and damaging intestinal epithelial cells,
increasing intestinal permeability and inflammation [ 48]. A rat model
showed that P. aeruginosa can spread via the bloodstream to the gall -
bladder, multiply and migrate to the intestines and feces, facilitating
transmission to other animals [ 49]. Its presence in the control group
suggests potential transmission among animals, despite the absence of
clinical symptoms at sampling.
The genus Pasteurella showed to be enriched in the diarrhea group.
Although it is widely known for its association with respiratory in -
fections, Pasteurella has also been described in weaned diarrheic pigs
[50], which reinforces that dysbiosis associated with post -weaning
diarrhea occurs in piglets.
Studies conducted in different regions, including those by Luo et al.
[40], Kong et al. [50], Panah et al. [35], Wang et al. [51], Grandmont
et al. [45] and our own, reveal consistent patterns in the gut microbiota
of weaned pigs, both healthy and with diarrhea. These findings suggest
that, despite geographic and management variations, universal fac-
tors—such as the transition to weaning and gut health play a key role in
shaping microbiota composition and function, highlighting the presence
of conserved biological mechanisms regulating gut microbial dynamics.
To further explore the microbiota’s role in both groups, we
performed a functional prediction analysis, revealing a higher abun -
dance of three aromatic compound degradation pathways (2 -amino-
phenol, 4 -chloronitrobenzene, and 4 -nitrotoluene II) in the diarrhea
group. According to PubChem (National Institutes of Health (NIH)), 2-
aminophenol is a bacterial metabolite with an aerobic metabolic pathway
described in Pseudomonas, Bordetella, and Burkholderia species [52].
Bordetella, a known user of this compound, is a causative agent of
atrophic rhinitis in pigs, often co-occurring with Pasteurella in infected
animals [53]. In our study, Pasteurella was the most enriched genus in
the diarrhea group. Given that it is excreted in feces, its high abundance
in these animals may reflect ongoing infection.
The degradation of the compounds 4 -chloronitrobenzene and 4 -
nitrotoluene, enriched in the diarrhea group, with genes identified in
Pseudomonas and Mycobacterium species [54]. These pathways allow
bacteria to use these compounds as a source of nitrogen, carbon, and
energy, releasing ammonia under aerobic conditions [ 55]. The meta -
bolic versatility of opportunistic bacteria, such as Pseudomonas aerugi-
nosa, contributes to their ability to colonize the gastrointestinal tract of
hosts.
Amos et al. [ 56] identified antimicrobial -resistant Pseudomonas in
pig feces, emphasizing its presence in the gastrointestinal tract and the
need for responsible antimicrobial use in pig farming. Although
P. aeruginosa is not directly linked to diarrhea in pigs, its role as an
opportunistic bacterium suggests it may contribute to intestinal dys -
biosis and exacerbate gastrointestinal disorders. Additionally, its ability
to metabolize nitroaromatic compounds may enhance intestinal persis -
tence and be associated with pathogenicity and colonization. This is
particularly relevant in weaning pigs with immature immune systems,
increasing their susceptibility to infecti ons.
The reductive tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle was also enriched in the
diarrhea group. According to the MetaCyc database, this pathway has
both anabolic and catabolic components. The TCA cycle primarily
converts fuel sources into energy, though several intermediates also
serve as precursors for biosynthetic processes, such a s the synthesis of
sugars, lipids and amino acids [ 57]. The cycle is tightly regulated by
physiological signals to optimize energy production and cellular func -
tion [ 58]. Stress from early weaning has been shown to reduce the
expression of proteins related to the TCA cycle, β -oxidation and
glycolysis in piglet enterocytes, particularly in the upper and middle
jejunal villi [ 59]. This may explain the increased activity of the TCA
reductase cycle in animals with diarrhea.
The metabolic pathway of trans-3-hydroxy-L-proline was enriched in the
control group. This pathway is related to L-proline degradation [60].
Hydroxyproline (Hyp), an amino acid abundant in sow’s milk, has
antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. It is a precursor to glycine
and is metabolized by intestinal microorganisms via the enzyme hy -
droxyproline dehydratase (HypD) [ 61]. Tang et al. [ 62] demonstrated
that Hyp improves the intestinal health in weaned piglets by enhancing
the intestinal barrier integrity and regulating microbiota. This explains
the increased activity of this pathway in the control group, emphasizing
its role in maintaining homeostasis and metabolic adaptation.
The control group also showed enrichment in two metabolic path -
ways for L -lysine degradation, which varies among microorganisms,
animals, and plants. While many initial reactions are well-studied, some
subsequent steps remain poorly understood. These pathways involve up
to ten different routes for L -lysine degradation [ 54]. Lysine is an
essential amino acid involved in hormone, enzyme, and antibody pro -
duction, as well as calcium absorption, muscle formation, and recovery.
It also plays a key role in treating viral infections, anxiety, migraines,
mood disorders, Alzheimer’s, alopecia, and certain cardiovascular dis -
eases [63]. The enrichment of such pathways in control group indicates
that it may be related to the health status of the gut in pigs.
Additionally, in the control group, L -threonine degradation path -
ways were enriched. L-threonine is an essential amino acid that supports
aging prevention, immunity and disease resistance [ 64]. Deficiencies
can lead to immune disfunction and growth issues. L-threonine is widely

used in the food and pharmaceutical industries [64]. This amino acid is
especially provided for piglets and young poultry, among other animals.
In pig feeding, it is the second limiting amino acid, aiding growth, mucin
production for improved digestion and nutrient absorption, and playing
a key role in protein synthesis and energy metabolism [ 65].
Bacterial taxa and metabolic pathways associated with inflammatory
and pathogenic microorganisms were identified in diarrheic pigs, rein -
forcing the link between dysbiosis and gastrointestinal disorders. Dys -
biosis, characterized by reduced microbial diversity and the
predominance of pro -inflammatory taxa (e.g., Pseudomonadota), leads to
metabolic dysfunction, including decreased production of short -chain
fatty acids (SCFAs) and increased inflammatory metabolites [ 29]. The
transition from a liquid to a solid diet during weaning exacerbates these
changes, compromising the intestinal barrier, reducing mucin produc -
tion, and increasing epithelial [ 66]. Combined with the immaturity of
the gastrointestinal tract and immune system, these factors heighten
susceptibility to gastrointestinal diseases, emphasizing the need for
strategies to modulate microbiota and mitigate the effects of dysbiosis
[10].
This study has several limitations that should be considered. The
small sample size may restrict the generalizability of the findings, and
antibiotic use in both groups may have influenced the intestinal
microbiota. Additionally, the lack of detailed animal records such as sex,
diarrhea severity and exact onset, and the absence of pre -diarrhea
microbiota data limit the ability to assess microbial shifts. Lastly, the
absence of longitudinal follow -up prevents the analysis of microbiota
dynamics over time. Fu ture studies with larger sample sizes and
continuous monitoring could provide a more comprehensive under -
standing of these effects.

5. Conclusions

The results indicate that although there is no significant difference in
the overall bacterial composition in piglets with and without diarrhea, a
shift in the microbiota and metabolic pathways was detected in terms of
differential abundance. Most of the taxa enriched in the diarrhea group
were associated with inflammatory microorganisms involved in patho-
genic processes. Additionally, enriched metabolic pathways related to
bacterial metabolism were observed, suggesting increased microbial
activity that may be contributing to diarrhea condition.
In the control group, all enriched metabolic pathways are funda -
mental for pig development. Likewise, the enriched taxa identified in the
control group provides valuable insights for developing alternatives to
antibiotic use during the post -weaning phase. Implementing probiotics
or other feed additives capable of positively modulating the intestinal
microbiota could serve as a promising stra tegy to prevent diarrhea,
promote gut health, and enhance the zootechnical performance of pigs.
These findings are relevant for pig industry, especially in evaluated area,
since environmental conditions and management practices can directly
influence microbial composition.

Abstract
Post-weaning diarrhea in piglets represents a significant challenge in pig farming,
affecting animal health and economic viability. Although the bacterial microbiome has
been studied, the role of the intestinal virome in the pathogenesis of diarrhea remain s
poorly understood. This study characterized the gut virome of weaned piglets with and
without diarrhea aiming to identify viral signatures associated with this condition. There
were no significant differences in alpha diversity between groups, but beta d iversity
analysis revealed significant qualitative changes in viral composition. The group with
diarrhea showed an increase in the relative abundance of Bocaparvovirus and Rotavirus
A in differential abundance, both pathogenic eukaryotic viruses, and enrichment of
bacteriophages that infect commensal or opportunistic bacteria ( Junavirus,
Paclarkvirus), accompanied by a reduction in the relative abundance of regulatory
bacteriophages (Phixviricota/Microviridae). In contrast, healthy piglets had a viral
community dominated by regulatory bacteriophages ( Peduoviridae, Phitrevirus phi3 )
and commensal CRESS -DNA viruses (Porprismacovirus). Free-living amoeba viruses
were detected exclusively in the control group, suggesting differentiated environmental
exposure. It can be concluded that there is a reconfiguration of the intestinal virome in
post-weaning diarrhea, characterized by the pres ervation of overall viral diversity, but
with compositional changes where regulatory bacteriophages and commensal viruses are
replaced by a viral signature of pathogenicity and dysbiosis. The selective presence of
different viruses among the groups reinforces that components of the intestinal virome
may reflect different states of equilibrium in the intestinal ecosystem and the infl uence
of external factors.

Keywords: Viral metagenomics; gastrointestinal virome; swine virus; diarrhea; stress
weaning.

47

Introduction
Pig farming is a segment of significant importance in the global animal protein
market, pork being the second most consumed meat in the world (ABPA, 2024). Recent
projections by the OECD -FAO (2024) indicate an expansion trend of around 8% in
global consumption by 2033, corroborating its significant participation in the
international agro-industrial complex. Brazil has a prominent position in the production
and trade scenario and is the world's fourth largest producer and exporter (ABPA,
2024b). Modern pig farming adopts early weaning between two and four weeks of age,
significantly earlier than the natural period that would occur between 12 and 18 weeks
in the wild. This practice, although economically advantageous, presents considerable
challenges due to th e physiological immaturity of piglets, slowing down digestion and
absorption (Qin et al., 2024). The still -developing digestive and immune systems,
combined with the abrupt interruption of the supply of immunoglobulins and other
bioactive components of mot her's milk, result in increased susceptibility to pathogens
and intestinal disorders (St-Pierre et al., 2023).
Early weaning exacerbates stress in piglets, compromising the function of the
intestinal epithelial barrier and significantly increasing the risk of enteric dysfunctions.
It also causes electrolyte imbalances in the gastrointestinal tract, characterized by a
decrease in the expression of fluid absorption proteins and an increase in the expression
of secretion proteins (Tang et al., 2022). These changes lead to the accumulation of fluid
in the intestinal lumen and large intestine, often resulting in diarrhea that can progress to
severe cases with dehydration and mortality (Tao et al., 2022).
The gut microbiome forms a complex ecosystem where various microorganisms
interact and influence gut health. In a previous study conducted by our group, we
observed that the main change in the bacterial microbiota of animals with post-weaning
diarrhea lies in its composition (differential abundances), with no significant changes in
other general parameters of the bacterial community when compared to healthy animals
(Dias et al., 2025). This result highli ghted the importance of investigating other
components of the microbiome, especially the virome, as possibly altered in this
condition. Other studies have already demonstrated that viruses have the potential to

48
modulate both the composition and functionality of the bacterial microbiota through
complex interactions with host microorganisms, and can influence digestive,
immunological and inflammatory processes, significantly impacting the intestinal health
of piglets during the critical post-weaning period (Wang et al., 2023).
Although the role of viruses in the gut microbiome is not yet fully understood,
recent studies suggest that these agents can contribute to maintaining microbial balance
and strengthening the immune system (Zeng et al., 2024). Bacteriophages stand out in
this context because they significantly influence the composition and functions of the
bacterial microbiota. In addition, these viruses act as modulators of the immune response,
participating in the regulation of innate, humoral and cell -mediated immunity (Leonard
& Toro, 2023).
Considering the challenges faced during the weaning phase in pig farming, this
study aimed to characterize the intestinal viral communities of piglets with and without
diarrhea on a farm in southern Brazil. We sought to describe the viral diversity of thes e
animals and investigate the relationship between the virome and intestinal health, to
identify possible correlations with enteric disorders.

Materials and methods

Ethical approval
This study was approved by the UFRGS Animal Use Ethics Committee (CEUA,
protocol 33558/2018), strictly following animal welfare standards to minimize animal
discomfort and suffering.

Experimental design
The study was conducted with 30 weaned Duroc piglets, aged 33 days old in
the nursery phase, from a certified swine breeding farm (CSBF) in Rio Grande do Sul,
Brazil. Convenience sampling included 15 animals with diarrhea, characterized by the
presence of liquid feces, and 15 healthy animals as a control group, randomly selected
from those without clinical signs of diarrhea. The diarrheic piglets were kept together in
the same pen, while the healthy animals were distributed in groups of 10 individuals per

49
pen. The sample size was determined by the availability of animals with symptoms at
the time of collection, maintaining numerical parity between the groups to ensure
comparability in the analysis.

Food and health management
The nutritional and health protocol for the animals was implemented at two
critical stages of development. During the dietary transition phase, at 15 days of age, the
piglets received a pre-starter diet formulated with highly digestible ingredients, including
fish meal, milk powder, soy, and corn, supplemented with a vitamin -mineral complex,
probiotics, prebiotics, and antioxidants to strengthen the immune system and promote
intestinal health.
During the weaning period, established at 28 days of age, a comprehensive
vaccination schedule was implemented, with the application of three immunobiologicals:
autogenous vaccine against Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae (Microvet, Brazil),
M+PAC for Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae (MSD Animal Health, USA), and Circumvent
PCV against porcine circovirus type 2 (MSD Animal Health, USA). In addition, a
preventive therapeutic regimen was adopted that included the administration of
Norfloxacin 14 mg/kg (Farmaflox®, Farmabase™, Brazil) in drinking water between 21
and 28 days of age, as well as a single intramuscular dose of Tulathromycin 2.5 mg/kg
(Draxin®, Zoetis™, USA).

Sample collection and storage
Rectal swabs were collected from all the animals (n = 15 per group) and placed
in sterile tubes containing 400 μL of RNALater® (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The
samples were transported on ice on the same day as collection and stored at -70 °C until
processing in the laboratory.

Sample processing and Viral nucleic acid extraction
The swabs with RNALater® were thawed and 800 μL of phosphate -buffered
saline (PBS) were added. The samples were homogenized in sterile tubes containing
sterile ceramic beads using a shaking device (Precellys® 24 - Bertin Technologies S.A.S,

50
Versailles, France), three times at 5,500 rpm for 20 seconds, with 30 second intervals
between each cycle. For the extraction of viral nucleic acids, the samples were
individually filtered with sterile 0.45 μm filters and centrifuged at 130,000 x g for 2 h at
4 ºC on 25% sucrose cushions. Prior to filtration and centrifugation, sample volumes
were adjusted with PBS to at least 5 mL. The supernatant was discarded and the resulting
pellet was resuspended in 200 μL of ultrapure water and treated with endonucleases by
adding 25 μL of DNAse buffer (Thermo Scientific), 5 μL of RNAse (Thermo Scientific)
and 2 μL of turbo DNAse (Thermo Scientific). The samples were incubated for 2 hours
at 37 ºC. Enzyme inactivation was performed by adding EDTA to a final concentration
of 15 mM, followed by heating at 75°C for 10 minutes. The nucleic acids were
subsequently extracted with MagMAX Pathogen DNA/RNA purification kit (Life
Technologies, Inc.), according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Nucleic acid enrichment e virome sequencing
Viral DNA was enriched by multiple displacement amplification (MDA) using
ϕ29 DNA polymerase, as described by Dean et al. (2002). Viral RNA was enriched using
REPLI-g WTA Single Cell Kit (Qiagen), following the manufacturer's instructions. The
enriched nucleic acids were quantified using the Qubit ™ dsDNA HS Assay Kit on a
Qubit 2.0 Fluometer (Invitrogen, Life technologies) and subsequently combined in
equimolar amounts. The mixture was purified using the Agencourt AMPure XP
(Beckman Coulter), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Library preparation was
performed using the Nextera XT DNA Library Prep kit (Illumina), and sequencing was
carried out on the Illumina Miseq platform using the Miseq Reagent kit v2 500 cycles
(Illumina), generating 2 x 250 bp.

Bioinformatics analysis
The quality of the raw sequences was assessed by FastQC (phred score <20) and
filtered with Trimmomatic to remove adapters, low-quality regions and short reads (<50
bp), with final re-evaluation by FastQC to ensure reliable data. For viral identification,
the reads were aligned to the Viral RefSeq database using DIAMOND in blastx mode,
with optimized parameters (E -value ≤1e-5, best hit per sequence and 40 threads). The

51
tabular result included alignment metrics and taxonomic IDs, allowing efficient viral
classification without additional annotation steps. This approach ensured a sensitive and
specific analysis, even for large volumes of data.

Relative abundance
The data normality and homogeneity of variances were accessed by Shapiro -
Wilk and Levene tests. The relative abundance of viruses among the experimental groups
was compared using the Mann -Whitney U test. To characterize the dominant viral
profile, a descen ding ranking of the 10 most abundant taxa at each taxonomic level
(Family, Genus, and Species) was performed, allowing the identification of the main
viral representatives in both experimental conditions.

Alpha and beta diversities
The alpha diversity indices (viral richness, Shannon, Simpson, and Pielou) were
calculated using the vegan package. All indices were previously subjected to normality
(Shapiro-Wilk) and homoscedasticity (Levene) tests. Based on this assessment, the viral
richness and Pielou uniformity indices, which met the parametric criteria, were analyzed
using Student's t -test, while the Shannon and Simpson indices, which did not have
normal distribution, were evaluated using the Mann-Whitney U test.
For beta diversity, two dissimilarity metrics were applied: Bray -Curtis (relative
abundance) and Jaccard (presence/absence). The method comprised the calculation of
distance matrices, followed by principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) to visualize
dissimilarity patterns. The stati stical significance of differences between groups was
determined using the PERMANOVA test with 9,999 permutations, with graphical
representation limited to PCoA plots, which included confidence ellipses and statistical
annotations.

Differential abundance
Differential abundance analysis was performed using the DESeq2 package. The
standardized workflow included: preprocessing with low -count filtering (<10 reads),
normalization by size factors, dispersion estimation, and Wald testing. Strict significance

52
criteria (p-value < 0.05 and FDR < 0.1) were adopted to identify differentially abundant
rates at multiple taxonomic levels (Family, Genus, Species). The results were visualized
in horizontal bar charts and exported in appropriate formats to ensure transpa rency and
analytical reproducibility.

Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed in the R environment (R Core Team, 2025),
using an integrated approach that included analyses of relative abundance (Mann -
Whitney U test), alpha diversity (Student's t -test and Mann -Whitney U test), beta
diversity (PERMANOVA with four dissimilarity metrics), and differential abundance
(DESeq2). Data manipulation used the dplyr, tidyr, and stringr packages; graphical
visualizations were developed with ggplot2 and ggforce; ecological analyses employed
vegan; and phylogenetic analyses used phyloseq and ape. The level of significance was
set at p ≤ 0.05.

Results
Relative abundance
Metagenomic sequencing of the 30 samples (15 Control and 15 Diarrhea)
generated 4,616,790 raw reads. After quality filtering, 49.83% of the sequences
(2,300,618 reads) were retained for analysis, of which 11.59% (266,653 reads) were
identified as viral. The Diarrhea group showed a higher average proportion of viral reads
(13.95%) compared to the Control group (10.22%), with samples D2 (32.86%) and D7
(32.77%) exhibiting the highest viral loads (Supplementary Table S1). Taxonomic
analysis revealed extensive viral diversity, comprising 14 phyla, 23 classes, 42 orders,
114 families, 1,185 genera, and 2,850 viral species.
At the Family level, the Control group showed dominance of Microviridae
(55.89%) and Smacoviridae (20.69%), followed by Parvoviridae (6.81%) and
Genomoviridae (2.04%). The Diarrhea group exhibited Parvoviridae (31.62%),
Microviridae (30.81%) and Smacoviridae (27.48%) as the most representative families
(Figure 1A).
Genus-level analysis revealed that the Control group was dominated by

53
Porprismacovirus (31.18%) and Bocaparvovirus (10.58%), with secondary
contributions from Astrithrvirus (5.10%) and Oengusvirus (3.47%). In the Diarrhea
group, Bocaparvovirus was the most abundant genus (40.24%), followed by
Porprismacovirus (28.97%) (Figure 1B).
At species-level, the Control group had greater abundance of species like Lepus
americanus faeces (6.59%) and Lynx canadensis associated (5.72%), while the Diarrhea
group was characterized by Bocaparvovirus ungulate 5 (12.23%) and Porcine associated
porprismacovirus (12.14%) (Figure 1C).

Differential abundance
At the family level, only two taxa showed significant differential signatures:
Genomoviridae (log₂FC = +2.54; padj = 0.042) was enriched in the Diarrhea group,
while Peduoviridae (log₂FC = -1.59; padj = 0.074) was enriched in the Control group
(Figure 4A). At the genus level, eleven significant taxa were identified, notably
Rotavirus (log₂FC = +4.31; padj = 0.003) and Samwavirus (log₂FC = +4.20; padj =
0.0004) as enriched in Diarrhea, while Dagavirus (log₂FC = -2.83; padj = 0.00003) and
Mieseafarmvirus (log₂FC = -3.09; padj = 0.097) were more abundant in the Control
group (Figure 4B). The species -level analysis revealed the greatest diversity of
signatures, with eighteen differentially abundant viruses, including Lactobacillus phage
phiPYB5 (log₂FC = +4.58; padj = 0.007) and Fur seal feces associated circular DNA
virus (log₂FC = +4.01; padj = 0.0009) enriched in Diarrhea group, and Porprismacovirus
macas1 (log₂FC = -3.81; padj = 0.002) and Phitrevirus phi3 (log₂FC = -3.36; padj =

Discussion
Comparison of the virome between post-weaning diarrhea and the control groups
revealed distinct viral profiles. The phylum Phixviricota, dominant in relative abundance
in the control group, is composed mainly of bacteriophages of the family Microviridae,
small single -stranded circular DNA (ssDNA) viruses with ubiquitous distribution in
aquatic environments and the gastrointestinal tract. Their relevance in intestinal
homeostasis is linked to genera such as those of the subfamily Bullavirinae, which

57
includes Alphatrevirus, Gequatrovirus, and Sinsheimervirus , specialized in infecting
enterobacteria. By modulating these bacterial communities, these phages contribute to
the regulation of the intestinal ecosystem (Kurilovich & Geva -Zatorsky, 2025). This
profile was complemented by the detection of viruses belonging to the phyla Uroviricota
and Cressdnaviricota. These groups include circular single -stranded DNA viruses
(CRESS-DNA), often found in fecal samples from pigs (Qian et al., 2024). In contrast,
the group with diarrhea showed a reduction in the relative abundance of the phyla
Phixviricota and Uroviricota and the family Microviridae, suggesting a loss of
microbiota modulation by phages (Fehér et al., 2021). At the same time, there was an
increase in the phylum Cossaviricota, especially in the family Parvoviridae and the
genus Bocaparvovirus, commonly associated with gastroenteritis (Qian et al., 2024).
In the samples from the diarrhea group, the pathogens that stood out with the
highest relative abundance at the species level were Bocaparvovirus ungulate 5 and
Porcine bocavirus 5 . This finding highlights the relevance of these agents in swine
enteric conditions and, considering their reported detection in multiple species,
corroborates the importance of a One Health approach to understanding their
epidemiology, potential for circulation between hosts, and impact on animal production
(Prpić et al., 2024; Sarchese et al., 2024). These viruses belong to the family
Parvoviridae, have a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) genome and a remarkable range of
hosts, including mammals, birds, and insects (Anoyatbekova et al., 2025). While
classical Protoparvovírus ungulate1 remains the leading cause of reproductive disorders
(Vargas-Bermudez et al., 2025), our results reinforce the potential role of
bocaparvoviruses in the etiology of diarrhea. Porcine bocaparvoviruses, first identified
in Sweden in 2009 (Blomström et al., 2 009), are now recognized as global pathogens
associated with gastrointestinal and respiratory syndromes . These viruses are often
described in co-infections with agents such as PCV2, PEDV, and PRRSV (Liu et al.,
2024; Tan et al., 2022). The ability of porcine bocaparvovirus to act as a primary
pathogen was recently demonstrated in the Harbin (China) outbreak (Ji et al., 2025).
Although Porcine bocavirus 5 has been reported in studies since 2012 (Li et al., 2012),
it remains unclassified and is not listed in the ICTV. The detection of Bocaparvovirus
ungulate 5 and Porcine bocavirus 5 in our study suggests that these viruses may be

58
relevant to post -weaning diarrhea, although they are probably not the only etiological
agent and may act in association with other detected viruses. Thus, they deserve greater
attention in the farm environment, and further studies are needed to understand its
circulation among animals.
No significant differences in alpha diversity were detected between the control
and diarrhea groups, demonstrating the preservation of the overall structure of the viral
community. A previous study on the virome of weaned piglets with diarrhea also found
no differences in alpha diversity compared to healthy animals (Nantel -Fortier et al.,
2022). In contrast, our results of beta diversity analysis show a significant dissimilarity
by the Jaccard metric, which revealed a clear distinction between the groups b ased on
the presence or absence of viral taxa. It is important to note that the Bray -Curtis metric,
in turn, remained unchanged. These results indicate that diarrhea is mainly associated
with changes of specific viral taxa, without compromising the relativ e proportions of
dominant viruses in the community. This suggests that this is a characteristic dynamic of
the intestinal virome in diarrheal contexts and relevant for comparative investigations of
the virome between sick and healthy individuals (Tao et al., 2022). It is important to note
that all animals shared the same zootechnical profile (identical breed, growth stage, and
management protocol). This standardization is corroborated by a previous study by our
group, which also found no significant differences in intestinal bacterial microbiota
diversity (Dias et al., 2025). These data indicate that management can act to standardize
microbial communities, so the specific changes observed in the virome are more likely
attributable to the clinical condition of diarrhea.
In the diarrhea group, a significant increase in the Genomoviridae family was
observed, corroborating recent studies that associate these viruses with enteropathies in
pigs (Qian et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). Their previous detection in cases of human
diarrhea and in other species (Zhuang et al., 2023) suggests a pot ential gastrointestinal
tropism or association with dysbiosis through multiple hosts. In contrast, the control
group showed significant enrichment of the Peduoviridae family, tailed bacteriophages
such as phage P2, which infect Enterobacteriaceae such as Escherichia coli, Shigella
spp., and Salmonella spp. (Cunliffe et al., 2022; Fa-arun et al., 2023; Turner et al., 2023).
This profile suggests an ecological role for this phage group as a moderator of

59
enterobacterial populations in the healthy intestine.
At the genus level, Rotavirus A stood out as the most distinctive viral signature
in the diarrhea group, corroborating its recognized etiological role in piglet diarrhea,
although it was also detected in asymptomatic animals (Smoľak et al., 2022). The
circulation of multiple genotypes ( A, B, C, H) is widely documented (Krasnikov et al.,
2024; Puente et al., 2023), with genotypes A and C predominating in suckling and
weaned piglets (Strydom et al., 2024). Rotaviruses of genotype A (RVA), belonging to
the Reoviridae family, are characterized by high environmental resistance and tropism
for mature enterocytes of the small intestine (Staff, 2025). Infection causes villous
atrophy, malabsorption of nutrients, and osmotic diarrhea, resulting in dehydration,
weight loss, a nd, in severe cases, death (Carossino et al., 2024). In pig farming,
transmission occurs mainly via the fecal -oral route, with significant productive and
economic impact on suckling and weaned piglets. Additionally, pig herds can act as
reservoirs, with evidence of zoonotic transmission (Strydom et al., 2024). Control is
based on biosecurity, cleaning, and disinfection, although viral stability makes
eradication challenging. Vaccination of breeding stock is used to boost humoral
immunity and antibo dy transfer via colostrum, although overly strict health protocols
may limit natural exposure and modulate maternal immunity (Rybkowska et al., 2025).
In the diarrhea group, significant enrichment of the genera Junavirus,
Sukhumvitvirus, and Colunavirus was also observed, all of which are bacteriophages
specialized in Lactobacillus. This finding is relevant because, although Lactobacillus has
probiotic properties, its phages can act as vectors of virulence genes through the process
of lysogenic conversion (Lv et al., 2025). By integrating their genome into the bacterial
chromosome (forming a prophage), these phages can introduce factors th at increase
bacterial pathogenicity or convert non-pathogenic strains into pathogenic ones (Pei et al.,
2021), which may justify their association with the diarrheal condition.
The genus Kehishuvirus, composed of bacteriophages that infect bacteria of the
genus Bacteroides (fundamental components of the swine microbiota), was also
differentially enriched in the diarrhea group. Evidence in humans suggests that the
activity of these phages can beneficially modulate the intestinal ecosystem, suppress
inflammation and promote epithelial barrier homeostasis (Dinić et al., 2025). Their

60
enrichment in diarrheic animals may therefore represent a phage response to contain
bacterial populations involved in gastrointestinal injury. However further studies are
necessary to confirm this potential role.
In contrast, the control group showed enrichment of the genus Mieseafarmvirus
(species RSL1), temperate bacteriophages that infect Klebsiella pneumoniae. Their high
presence in asymptomatic animals suggests intestinal colonization by K. pneumoniae in
healthy pigs (Wareth & Neubauer, 2021). This profile could indicate a balanced phage -
bacteria interaction in vivo, a relevant hypothesis given the problem of antimicrobial
resistance associated with this species (Kot & Witeska, 2024). However, confirma tion
depends on integrated studies that directly correlate the dynamics of these phages with
the abundance and profile of K. pneumoniae in the same environment.
Among the species enriched in the control group, Porprismacovirus macas1 and
Porprismacovirus porci2 stand out. The genus Porprismacovirus, initially detected in
pigs and primates (Dai et al., 2024), has the widest host range in the Smacoviridae family
(Fehér et al., 2021). Complementarily, the genus Felismacovirus (from the same family)
showed enrichment in the diarrhea group. Both are frequently detected in fecal and
environmental samples, with no clear association with pathogenicity, and have been
described in healthy and sick animals (Liu et al., 2022).
The species Phitrevirus phi3 was enriched in the control group. This is a
bacteriophage specific to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and its enrichment corroborates to
previous bacteriological data from these same animals, which reported an increase in the
genus Pseudomonas in the control group (Dias et al., 2025). This bacteriophage has
documented circulation in Brazil (Xavier et al., 2025), and the presence of P. aeruginosa
in the gastrointestinal tract is feasible due to its ability to spread systemically, altho ugh
it is commonly more associated with the respiratory tract (Wood et al., 2023). Similarly,
the enrichment of the species Phabquatrovirus PHB04 in the control group, a
bacteriophage that infects Bordetella bronchiseptica, suggests a modulatory role in the
intestinal environment. Although it is a primary respiratory pathogen, B. bronchiseptica
can cause gastrointestinal lesions in pigs (Yang et al., 2022), and phage therapy has been
shown to be effective in controlling it (Hosseindoust et al., 2023).
It is important to point out that this study has limitations inherent to its design

61
and the methodologies employed. The characterization of the virome itself is limited by
the scarcity of reference databases. In addition, the animals that manifested clinical
symptoms were immediately separated for treatment. Consequently, it was not possible
to correlate the microbial changes observed with the exact duration or severity of
individual diarrhea. Thus, the results represent a spot sampling of clinical states within a
controlled management context, and the inferences made are, by nature, corre lational
and indicative.

Conclusion
This study reveals that diarrhea in weaned piglets triggers a qualitative
restructuring of the intestinal virome, without a generalized reduction in its diversity.
Alpha diversity is maintained, along with a significant change in qualitative beta
diversity, indicating that diarrhea does not promote a generalized disruption of the viral
community, but rather a selective replacement of certain taxa, suggesting an ecological
filter effect that reshapes the viral composition. This reorganization is characterized by
the decline of regulatory bacteriophages and commensal viruses, while viruses
associated with pathogenicity and dysbiosis become predominant, outlining a distinct
viral signature of the diarrheal state. An increase in the relative abundance of
Bocaparvovirus in the diarrheal group was observed, indicating a need for further studies
to its detection in pig farms in evaluated area. We also identified an enrichment of
Rotavirus in the diarrhea group, an agent widely described as a cause of diarrhea in
weaned piglets and known for its high environmental resistance, which makes control in
farms difficult. Both viruses have zoonotic potential, and their presence represents an
occupational risk for farm workers and reinforces the need to implement more rigorous
sanitary measures.

6. DISCUSSÃO GERAL
A diarreia pós-desmame na suinocultura é um distúrbio de etiologia multifatorial,
envolvendo complexas interações entre o hospedeiro, ambiente e o microbioma intestinal.
Para elucidar os fatores microbianos envolvidos na patogênese, este estudo analisou a
microbiota bacteriana e o viroma de leitões diarreicos e saudáveis. Apesar da diversidade
global da microbiota se manter estável, identificamos alterações pontuais e significativas
na composição de ambos os componentes nos animais doentes. Tais descobertas
fornecem evidências que podem auxiliar na compreensão sobre as disbioses bacterianas
e virais que possivelmente tenham relação com o surgimento da diarreia em leitões em
fase de desmame.
Nos animais com diarreia, observou -se um aumento na razão
Bacillota/Bacteroidota. Essa razão tem sido amplamente utilizada como biomarcador
de saúde intestinal (Karačić et al., 2024), embora sua interpretação seja complexa, uma
vez que estudos há estudos discordantes relacionados a diarreia e outras patologias
(Zhou et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2023) , assim como a redução dessa razão também já foi
caracterizada como benéfica para microbiota intestinal (Goggans et al., 2022).
Não foram detectadas alterações significativas na diversidade alfa da microbiota
bacteriana e do viroma intestinal, demonstrando a estabilidade da diversidade intrínseca
dessas comunidades microbianas, mesmo na presença de sinais clínicos. Em contraste, a
análise de diversidade beta revelou um perfil distinto: enquanto a composição bacteriana
permaneceu similar entre os grupos, o viroma exibiu uma separação significativa no
índice de Jaccard. Esse resultado aponta para uma dissimilaridade baseada na composição
qualitativa (presença/ausência) de vírus específicos nos animais diarreicos, mas sem
diferença nas proporções quantitativas virais.
Na abundância diferencial o grupo controle apresentou um perfil composto por
bactérias com propriedades probióticas ( Liquorilactobacillus) (Liu et al., 2023 ) e
bactérias fermentadoras (Komagataeibacter, Acetobacter e Gluconobacter), que auxiliam
na digestão dos alimentos e atuam na modulação intestinal (Choi et al., 2022). Também
foram observadas bactérias oportunistas enriquecidas (Escherichia/Shigella, Salmonella,
Pseudomonas), indicando uma possível colonização controlada (Wang et al., 2021) . Já

71
em relação os vírus enriquecidos, foi observado no grupo controle bacteriófagos de
enterobactérias ( Peduviridae) e outros bacteriófagos de bactérias respiratórias que já
foram descritos presentes no trato gastrointestinal ( Phitrevirus phi3 e Phabquatrovirus
PHB04), a presença desses bacteriófagos sugere um papel ativo no controle de bactérias
oportunista e equilíbrio da comunidade microbiana, auxiliando na homeostase intestinal
(Cunliffe et al., 2022; Wood et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2022) .
Em contraste, no grupo diarreia estavam enriquecidas bactérias com potencial
inflamatório (Fusobacterium) e outra bactéria respiratória já descrita em leitões diarreicos
(Pasteurella), mostrando a presença de bactérias oportunistas, que podem intensificar
quadros de diarreia em suínos (Kong et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2022) . Em relação aos vírus
mais abundantes, destacou -se o enriquecimento Rotavirus A, com etiologia já bem
descrita na literatura em leitões diarreicos, que além de possuir grande resistência
ambiental também tem potencial zoonótico (Staff, 2025; Strydom et al., 2024).
Além disso, o aumento da abundância relativa no grupo diarreia de
Bocaparvovirus ungulate 5 e Porcine bocavirus 5, agentes emergentes presentes em casos
de diarreia em diversas espécies de hospedeiros, incluindo humanos, mostra a necessidade
de uma abordagem One Health para compreender melhor a patogenia desse grupo viral
(Prpić et al., 2024). Bocaparvovirus já foram descritos em muitos trabalhos atuando em
conjunto com outros vírus em casos de diarreia (Liu et al., 2024) , porém um estudo
recente chinês mostrou a presença desse vírus como único agente em um surto de diarreia
em suínos (Ji et al., 2025). Essas evidências destacam a necessidade de se implementarem
técnicas diagnósticas mais específicas para esse agente e de mais estudos para
compreender a circulação, patogenicidade e o papel clínico preciso desses vírus.
Esta tese apresenta limitações em duas frentes principais. Na caracterização
clínica, não foi possível obter registros detalhados sobre a evolução dos sintomas,
especialmente o tempo de duração da diarreia, o que dificulta a correlação entre o quadro
clínico e os agentes infecciosos identificados. Nas análises de bioinformática, não foi
realizada a montagem dos genomas virais a partir dos dados de sequenciamento e uma
análise conjunta da microbiota bacteriana e viral. Essas lacunas restringem uma
compreensão mais completa das interações entre os patógenos e abrem caminho para
investigações futuras que combinem dados clínicos refinados com abordagens integradas

72
de metagenômica.
7. CONCLUSÕES
Este trabalho identificou diferenças pontuais, porém significativas, na composição
bacteriana e viral entre leitões saudáveis e com diarreia pós -desmame, apontando para
possíveis causas microbianas específicas associadas ao quadro clínico. Foi observada
uma distinção na composição dos perfis microbianos, com o grupo saudável apresentando
uma comunidade bacteriana e viral potencialmente protetora e o grupo doente exibindo o
enriquecimento de bactérias oportunistas e vírus entéricos, reforça ndo a complexa
interação entre esses componentes na saúde e na doença em leitões em fase de desmame.
Não foram encontradas diferenças na diversidade alfa (microbiota e viroma) nem
na composição bacteriana (beta). Porém, a presença/ausência de vírus diferiu
significativamente entre os grupos, indicando que a diarreia pode estar associada a uma
alteração específica no perfil viral, sem mudanças expressivas nas comunidades
bacterianas.
O perfil metabólico funcional bacteriano também divergiu entre os grupos. No
grupo saudável, as vias predominantes sustentam funções fisiológicas e de crescimento.
Já nos leitões diarreicos, observou -se o enriquecimento de vias metabólicas bacterianas
específicas, indicando uma maior atividade ba cteriana que pode estar intensificando a
patogênese da diarreia.
A detecção de agentes com reconhecido potencial zoonótico , como Rotavirus
A e Bocaparvovirus, somada à presença de patógenos zoonóticos oportunistas, como
Fusobacterium, transcendem o âmbito da saúde animal e reforça a necessidade de uma
abordagem One Health para compreender a patogênese, a circulação e o impacto
epidemiológico desses patógenos. A identificação de tais microrganismos em suínos
destaca a interface entre a saúde animal e a saúde pública. Portanto, estratégias futuras de
vigilância, prevenção e controle devem ser estudadas, reconhecendo que a elucidação das
interações dinâmicas entre microbiota e viroma é fundamental tan to para a sanidade
suinícola quanto para a saúde global.
